Skip
skip
v.i. (to leap lightly; to bound)
Of Northern origin, akin to Old Norse skopa, to run. The Authorized Version uses it only of creation and of Christ: mountains skipping like rams, Lebanon skipping like a calf, and the Beloved leaping upon the mountains.

Biblical Definition

Every occurrence is a picture of joy in something too large to be moved. In the psalm of the voice of the LORD, the cedars break and then the mountains dance: “He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn” (Psalm 29:6). The Exodus psalm asks the mountains to explain themselves: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs” (Psalm 114:4), and then, turning to address them directly, “Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs?” (Psalm 114:6). The answer the psalm gives is that the earth trembled at the presence of the Lord. Then the Song sets the same verb on the Bridegroom: “The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song of Solomon 2:8). What the mountains do before God, the Beloved does upon the mountains — nothing in the landscape slows him when he comes for his bride.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines skip as to leap; to bound; to spring; to pass over lightly; and also, to pass without notice.

expand to see more

SKIP, v.i. To leap; to bound; to spring; as a goat or lamb.

SKIP, v.i. To pass over or omit anything in reading or writing.

SKIP, v.t. To pass over or by; to omit; to miss.

BOUND, v.i. To leap; to jump; to spring; to move forward by leaps.

EXULT, v.i. To rejoice in triumph; to rejoice exceedingly at success or victory.

Key Scripture

Psalm 29:6 — "He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn."

Psalm 114:4 — "The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs."

Psalm 114:6 — "Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs?"

Song of Solomon 2:8 — "The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills."

Modern Corruption

Nature is treated either as a machine that cannot respond or as a divinity to be worshipped; Scripture makes the hills glad before their Maker without ever confusing them with him.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors crowd around a verse like Psalm 114:4. The first is a flattened naturalism in which the creation is mere mechanism, and the poetry of skipping mountains is a pretty way of saying nothing. The second is the sacralizing of nature itself, in which the earth is a mother and creation the object rather than the choir of worship. Scripture holds a third thing steadily: the hills really do rejoice, the trees of the field clap their hands, and every bit of it is directed at the presence of the Lord, who made them and is not one of them.

The Song supplies the reason such joy is not sentimental. The same verb that moves mountains describes the Beloved coming for his bride — leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills — and the barriers that would stop anyone else are what he travels on. The mountains skip because God is present; the Bridegroom skips because his bride is waiting. A creation that exults before its Maker and a Saviour who comes swiftly for his people are the same doctrine viewed from two sides, and the right response to both is the psalm's: tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew raqad (H7540), to skip about, to dance; ayil (H352), a ram; chuwl (H2342), to writhe or tremble; dalag (H1801), to leap.

expand to see more

Hebrew raqad (H7540) — to stamp, to spring about, to dance; the skipping of Psalm 114:4.

Hebrew ayil (H352) — a ram; the figure for the mountains at Sinai.

Hebrew dalag (H1801) — to leap, to spring; the Beloved leaping upon the mountains.

Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to twist, to writhe, to tremble; the earth at the presence of the Lord.

Hebrew qowl (H6963) — a voice; the voice of the LORD that breaks cedars, and of the Beloved.

Usage

"“He maketh them also to skip like a calf” — Lebanon at the voice of the LORD."

"“The mountains skipped like rams” — and the psalm asks them why."

"“Leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” — the Bridegroom's speed."
